source.title: nanoLM: an Affordable LLM Pre-training Benchmark via Accurate Loss Prediction across Scales
source.authors: Yiqun Yao; Si-Qi Fan; Xiu-Sheng Huang; Xue-Zhi Fang; Xiang Li; Zi-Yi Ni; Xin Jiang; Xu-Ying Meng; Peng Han; Shuo Shang; Kang Liu; Aixin Sun; Yequan Wang

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses its own experiments to test power-law fitting and loss prediction across model sizes, but uses µP-based hyperparameter transfer rather than reproducing the original scaling-law methods. Its reported outcome is training loss, not held-out loss.
record.gate_note: The experiments report training loss, not held-out cross-entropy or validation loss. The paper discusses downstream performance and validation-loss correlation but does not measure downstream-task outcomes or held-out loss here. It cites other work on scaling laws but those cited results are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study fits L = aC^b + c of pretraining loss against parameter count on µP-transferred proxy models. It then extrapolates to larger targets (26B and 52B GPT, plus 12-layer GPT/Llama/BERT/T5) and compares with the actually trained loss. This is a different method (µP hyperparameter transfer) aimed at the same questions as V1 and V2. It also reports how fits depend on parametrization, hyperparameter basin, embedding counting and proxy averaging (V7). The record excluded V1 and V2 because the loss is training loss. However, the paper states training is under one epoch, so training loss tracks held-out loss, as Kaplan et al. also note. That makes the results bear on V1 and V2, with a caveat on the measure.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that µP plus a power law in total parameters (embeddings included) predicts the pretraining loss of larger models from small proxies, up to 52B, at about 14% of one training run's cost. They add that the fit holds only near the hyperparameter loss basin, and that very small proxies benefit from averaging. They also argue µP is sufficient but not necessary for scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Combines µP-based hyperparameter transfer with a fitted power law in parameter count; the paper counts embeddings in model size and tests prediction using training loss. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law experiments or their held-out-loss measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported fit behavior depends on whether hyperparameters are inside the low-loss basin, whether embeddings count toward model size, and whether nearby hyperparameter losses are averaged for very small proxy models. The paper also reports that no-µP fits are poorer.
record.code_released: not stated (the paper says it will open-source the code and data, but gives no repository URL)
record.problems: The reported loss is training loss rather than held-out or validation loss. Prediction experiments cover specific architectures, datasets, and training durations; the paper notes that the number of proxy points affects fit accuracy and uses seven points in one setting due to computational limits. Several sensitivity results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The MC4 table reports values at all eight widths for four models; only one aggregate width-sweep row per model is included, preserving all listed values. Other hyperparameter-specific curves in Figures 5 and 6 are summarized where the text explicitly describes their fit behavior.

untested.parts: Power laws in tokens or compute. Here tokens are fixed and short (7k–20k steps), so data may be a bottleneck absorbed into c.
Extrapolation over several orders of magnitude: the maximum gap is ~15x beyond the largest proxy.
Entirely untested; no compute-optimal split is studied.
Entirely untested; depth is varied only across separate series, not at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer (MC4 is still text).
Entirely untested; no downstream tasks are measured.
Dependence of the compute-optimal split, and the effects of schedule or data on exponents.

missing.what: Fit-error and coefficient-covariance comparison of nanoLM vs Cerebras-GPT, Cerebras-GPT+µP and Pythia. It shows the µP variant with lower prediction error (0.004 vs 0.034). The comparison partly reuses others' published losses.
Numeric power-law fits and predictions for the MC4 runs and for the 7k-step 12-layer fits; these are shown only in figures.

record.verdict_notes: Several printed fit coefficients are internally inconsistent with the losses and predictions. GPT and BERT have c above the observed or predicted losses, and T5's coefficients duplicate the 64-layer GPT fit. Verdicts therefore rest on the predicted vs actual loss values, not the coefficients. Training loss is treated as a held-out proxy because data is seen for under one epoch, but no validation loss is reported. The BERT no-µP table (r12) contradicts the text's claim that non-µP runs underperform.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports training loss rather than held-out pretraining loss; it does not test the stated held-out measure.
The extrapolations are for training loss, not held-out loss. No held-out-loss prediction is evaluated.
No fixed-compute search for an optimal parameter/token split, or scaling of that split with compute, is reported.
The study compares architecture variants but does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The study includes multilingual text data and several Transformer architectures, but does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance is measured against scale or pretraining loss.

The study examines dependence on hyperparameter choices, embedding parameter counting, and proxy-model fitting in training-loss experiments. It does not test compute-optimal allocation exponents or systematically compare all the setup and fitting choices named in the version.

statements.correction: Six-layer GPT: selected point (5e-4, 0.02, 3.5) fits well; nearby points show larger deviations than 12-layer models; averaging nearby losses improves fitting. Off-basin hyperparameters generalize poorly.
statements.problem: Very small proxies do not uniformly break the law: one selected hyperparameter point fits well, nearby points deviate more, and averaging restores the fit.
